flashcards.q: What's the core difference between how Dyna-Q and MCTS each use a model?
flashcards.a: Dyna-Q uses the model to generate additional SIMULATED training data between real interactions (extra Q-learning updates); MCTS uses the model to SEARCH AHEAD at decision time, building a tree of possible futures before committing to one real action, then discarding it and replanning.

flashcards.q: Write the UCT selection formula and explain what the sqrt(ln N(s)/N(s,a)) term controls.
flashcards.a: UCT(s,a) = Q(s,a) + c*sqrt(ln N(s)/N(s,a)). It's a confidence-interval width from UCB1: shrinks as N(s,a) grows (more evidence for this child), grows slowly (log) with N(s), preventing permanent abandonment of a child after an unlucky early run of simulations.

flashcards.q: Name MCTS's four phases in order.
flashcards.a: Selection (walk down via UCT/PUCT to an expandable node), Expansion (add a new leaf), Simulation/rollout (estimate the leaf's value), Backpropagation (push the result up every node on the path, updating visit counts and averages).

flashcards.q: What two structural changes does AlphaZero make relative to classic MCTS?
flashcards.a: 1) Replaces random rollouts with a learned value/policy network's direct estimate (lower variance, one forward pass instead of a full random playout). 2) Replaces UCT's plain exploration term with PUCT, which weights exploration by the policy network's prior over actions.

flashcards.q: Write the PUCT formula and explain why the prior term p(s,a) matters especially for Go.
flashcards.a: PUCT(s,a) = Q(s,a) + c*p(s,a)*sqrt(sum_b N(s,b))/(1+N(s,a)). Go's branching factor (~250) is far larger than chess's (~35); the prior concentrates the finite simulation budget on promising branches instead of uniformly exploring every action, which pure UCT would waste enormous budget doing at that branching factor.

flashcards.q: Why is compounding model error a fundamentally different problem from one-step model prediction error?
flashcards.a: One-step accuracy says nothing about whether errors compound benignly or catastrophically over a multi-step rollout -- divergence grows roughly with horizon times per-step error in a favorable case, and worse when small errors push the trajectory into regions the model has little accurate data for (increasingly out-of-distribution for the model itself).

flashcards.q: Why does MCTS commit to only one real action per search rather than executing its full simulated line?
flashcards.a: Committing to only the immediate next action and replanning fresh from the new, actually-observed state means deeper, less-explored, more error-prone parts of the tree never get executed blindly -- this bounds compounding model/opponent-uncertainty error to roughly one search's depth instead of an open-loop plan.

flashcards.q: Is Dyna-Q's simulated-update sample efficiency gain 'free' with no downside compared to pure model-free Q-learning?
flashcards.a: No -- simulated updates are only as good as the learned model's accuracy. A poor model (common early in training or in rarely-visited states) trains the value function toward a systematically wrong target, the same 'stable loss, wrong targets' failure signature as DQN.

flashcards.q: Why did Go resist strong AI play for decades longer than chess, beyond just compute cost?
flashcards.a: Go's branching factor (~250) is much larger than chess's (~35), making brute-force search far more expensive -- but more fundamentally, no good hand-crafted evaluation function existed for Go positions the way material/positional heuristics worked for chess, leaving even affordable search with nothing reliable to evaluate leaves with.

flashcards.q: What real numbers characterize AlphaZero's search budget and Go/chess branching factors?
flashcards.a: AlphaZero used roughly 800 simulations per move in self-play training. Go's branching factor is roughly 250 legal moves per position versus chess's roughly 35.

flashcards.q: What's the standard mitigation for compounding model error in practical model-based control systems?
flashcards.a: Short planning/rollout horizon combined with frequent replanning against fresh real observations (MPC-style), rather than committing to a long, open-loop plan purely from the model -- model-based rollout accuracy typically degrades sharply past roughly 5-15 steps in continuous-control benchmarks.
